_comment: Settlement Program canon — period-grounded settlement morphology for build_settlement. The settlement-tier analog of room_program.json: eras -> tiers (hamlet/village/town/city), each tier one preset of ONE layout algorithm family (Forge rule: one algorithm, many data presets). Units = CUBES (1 cube = 1 m). Every value carries a `sources` entry (the grounding rule); values without a real citation are flagged REASONED or NEEDS-RESEARCH inline — never silently invented.
_units: cubes (metres). street.main_width / lane_width are paved widths; plot.depth_* is the toft depth back from the street; setback is the yard between street edge and building front.
_era_hook: Top-level `eras` map is the extension point: a future era (e.g. iron_age, renaissance) adds its own tiers WITHOUT C++ changes. Only `medieval` ships; the loader must surface an unknown era as an ERROR, never silently default.

hamlet.description: A loose farming cluster — a handful of dwellings with no formal street; paths connect the crofts.

sources.morphology: dispersed hamlet / farm-cluster settlement form: Roberts, Rural Settlement in Britain (1977) — 'hamlet' = a cluster lacking the row/green plan-form of a village; matches the shipped terrain-scatter placement
sources.buildings: REASONED: 'a few households' — no hard count in the sources consulted; 3-6 chosen so a hamlet reads smaller than the smallest row village. NEEDS-RESEARCH (Roberts & Wrathmell, An Atlas of Rural Settlement in England, 2000)
sources.typology_weights: peasant-dominated mix: crofts + longhouses are the excavated dwelling stock at Wharram Percy (Beresford & Hurst); a lone hall_house = the yeoman holding. Ratio REASONED, not counted from a specific site plan
sources.plot.depth: toft (house-yard) depths 'tens of metres', scale-compressed to the settlement footprint — DESIGN DECISION disclosed; burgage/toft depth cite: Tait, PSAS 138 (2009) via room_program.json shop entries
sources.street.material: unpaved rural tracks — paving in rural hamlets is unattested; Dirt is the honest surface (REASONED)

village.description: A row/street village — dwellings front a single main street on both sides (toft-and-croft rows), with the tavern and smith among them.

sources.morphology: row/street village plan-form: Wharram Percy itself is a two-row village of tofts fronting a street (Beresford & Hurst, Wharram Percy: Deserted Medieval Village) — the same source that grounds the croft/longhouse typologies
sources.buildings: REASONED band between hamlet and market town; Wharram Percy's rows held ~30 tofts at peak, scale-compressed here. NEEDS-RESEARCH for a small-village count (Roberts & Wrathmell 2000)
sources.street.main_width: NEEDS-RESEARCH: no measured medieval village street width sourced yet. 5 m ≈ 'two carts can pass' convention cited for town royal-road widths (candidate: Salzman, Building in England; Schofield & Vince, Medieval Towns) — shipped FLAGGED, cite or record in GroundingGaps.md before phase close
sources.street.lane_width: NEEDS-RESEARCH: single-cart lane ~3 m REASONED from cart gauge ~1.5 m + clearance; same candidate sources as main_width
sources.street.material: REASONED: village streets were commonly unmade/gravelled; full stone paving is a town/burgage-era feature (Schofield & Vince note paving grants in TOWNS). Gravel = the modest middle
sources.plot.frontage: from_typology = burgage principle: plot width set by the building's frame width; frontage grounding rides on room_program.json width_max cites (Tait, PSAS 138 (2009): burgage frontages c. 5-17 m, modal 8 m)
sources.plot.depth: tofts extend back from the street row into crofts (Wharram Percy plan); 12-20 m is scale-compressed — DESIGN DECISION disclosed
sources.typology_weights: one tavern + one smith per small village is the classic service minimum (Medievalists.net inn record via room_program tavern entry; smith ubiquity REASONED); dwelling mix as hamlet. Weights REASONED, not censused
sources.public.well: shared village water source (well/spring) — common-provision REASONED; asset + placement land in Phase 3/4

town.description: A market town — cobbled main street widening into a market square, burgage rows with back lanes, shops among the dwellings.

sources.morphology: market town = main street + market place, burgage series with back lanes: Tait, PSAS 138 (2009) burgage-plot morphology; market places commonly a WIDENED main street (Schofield & Vince, Medieval Towns) — the Phase-4 square straddles the street per that form
sources.public.market_square.stalls: trestle stalls ('standings') on the market place: Schofield & Vince, Medieval Towns — count REASONED to the square's pad capacity
sources.street.material: town-street paving is attested (murage/pavage grants, Schofield & Vince) — Cobblestone is the settlement `dry_stone` sett material already in materials.json
sources.street.main_width: NEEDS-RESEARCH — same as village; town main streets wider than village (two carts + stalls)
sources.plot.side_gap: 0 = contiguous burgage series (party boundaries), per the burgage-row form (Tait 2009)
sources.setback: urban row-houses build to the street frontage line (setback 0-1): burgage frontage occupation, Tait 2009
sources.buildings: REASONED band; smallest boroughs were a few dozen burgages (Beresford, New Towns of the Middle Ages — NEEDS-RESEARCH for a specific count)
sources.public.market_square: 12x12 REASONED placeholder — Phase 4 grounds the square dims before building it
sources.typology_weights: full shop set appears at market-town tier (market function = the town's raison d'être); ratios REASONED

city.description: A walled-city quarter — crossroads axes meeting at a market square, jittered secondary streets slicing irregular blocks, trades clustered near the square. Slightly organized, a little chaotic.

sources.public.market_square.stalls: as town — trestle 'standings' on the place; count REASONED for a 16x16 square
sources.public.market_square.statue: DESIGN DECISION (fantasy setting): civic statue at the market-cross spot — the period-strict centrepiece is the market cross (docs/CityForgePlan.md M1)
sources.morphology: organic-accretion city form (pre-planned medieval growth): Schofield & Vince, Medieval Towns — street networks accreted from AXES + infill, not surveyed grids. Implementation: crossroads axes meeting at the market square + secondary streets at seeded-JITTERED intervals (the bounded chaos) — DESIGN DECISION disclosed
sources.buildings: REASONED: a city QUARTER at this engine's buildable scale, not a whole city
sources.street.main_width: NEEDS-RESEARCH — principal city streets carried through-traffic + encroachment; wider than town main streets
sources.blocks: REASONED 18-30 m secondary-street spacing: burgage depth (12-18) + circulation; no measured medieval block-spacing source consulted yet (candidate: Conzen town-plan analysis, Alnwick) — NEEDS-RESEARCH
sources.core_typology_weights: market-adjacency of trades: shops/inns cluster on the market place and principal streets (Schofield & Vince; standard burgage-rent gradient reasoning) — ratios REASONED
sources.core_ring: REASONED ~24 m 'market frontage' radius — the first plot rows around the square; no measured source
sources.typology_weights: dwelling-heavy fringe mix + a manor_hall (urban magnate house); ratios REASONED
